summary: Volume is the amount of 3-D space inside a solid, found by packing it with unit cubes (1 cm³ each) with no gaps or overlaps and counting them. Learners build a cuboid from 1 cm³ cubes, see its layer structure (a layer holds rows×columns of cubes; the height tells how many layers, so count = cubes-per-layer × layers), account for the hidden lower layers that cannot be seen, and connect packing with cubes to filling with liquid (a box packed with 24 cm³ holds 24 ml of water). Packing volume is harder than iterating length or tiling area because it demands extending spatial structuring from two to three dimensions.
misconceptions: Counts only the visible cubes/faces and forgets the hidden lower layers — undercounting the 3-D array.
Adds the three dimensions (4+3+2) instead of building the layered array.
Treats the packed cubes as discrete objects, not as units of volume — doesn't see '24 cubes' as an amount of space.
Doesn't connect packing with filling — can't say how much water (ml) fills a box packed with 24 cm³ cubes.

activities.title: Pack a box layer by layer and reveal the hidden cubes
steps: Take an empty open box whose inside measures 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm and a pile of 1 cm³ cubes.
Before packing, predict how many cubes will fill the box completely and say WHY.
Lay the first layer as a 4-by-3 array and count it (12 cubes).
Stack the second layer on top and track the running count until it reads 24.
Rotate the box and open or lift the top layer to expose the bottom layer you could not see, confirming those hidden cubes still count.
State the count as cubes-per-layer × number-of-layers: 4×3 = 12 in a layer, 2 layers, 12×2 = 24.
State the result in cubic centimetres: 24 cm³.
activities.insight: Volume is a layered 3-D array: each layer holds rows×columns of cubes and the height gives the number of layers, so you multiply (or count layer by layer) and the hidden lower cubes count too. The answer is an amount of space measured in cubic units, not a heap of objects.

activities.title: Connect packing with cubes to filling with water
steps: Pack the same box completely with 1 cm³ cubes and agree on the count (24).

Empty it, then fill it with water poured from a cylinder marked in millilitres (the box must be watertight, or use a watertight container with the same inside measurements), and read how much water was poured in.
Compare the two results: the cubes show the box holds 24 cm³, and the water reading should be about 24 ml (small differences come from measuring and filling errors).
State the equivalence in your own words: 1 cm³ of water = 1 ml, so 24 cm³ = 24 ml.
Answer: 'If I filled this box with water instead of cubes, about how much water would it hold? How does that relate to the cubes?'
activities.insight: Packing (cubes) and filling (liquid) describe the same amount of space: because 1 cm³ = 1 ml, a box whose inside is exactly filled by 24 one-centimetre cubes (24 cm³) holds 24 ml of water, and a real pour should give about 24 ml. The cube count is a measure of volume, not a tally of separate objects.

activities.title: Predict the cube count from a net
steps: Look at the flat net of a box before it is folded or packed.
Predict how many 1 cm³ cubes will fill the assembled box, explaining your reasoning in terms of a layer and the number of layers.
Fold/assemble (or build) the box and pack it to check your prediction.
Reconcile any difference between prediction and result, naming where the reasoning went wrong.
activities.insight: The layer structure can be read off a box's net before packing: identify the cubes in one layer (length×width) and how many layers (height), then multiply — and verify by building.

activities.title: Estimate a container's capacity against a benchmark
steps: Pick a jug or container and estimate its capacity before measuring.
Compare it to a known 1-litre measure to judge whether it holds more or less, and roughly how much.
Pour to check against a graduated measure and state the capacity in millilitres or litres.
Relate capacity back to volume: discuss how a packed box's cm³ count would translate to ml.
activities.insight: Capacity can be estimated by comparison to a familiar benchmark (a 1-litre measure), and it connects to volume through the 1 cm³ = 1 ml relationship.

activities.title: Reference cutaway: the cubes you cannot see
steps: Study a cutaway picture of a packed cuboid that shows the interior cubes, including the bottom layer.
Mark or count the hidden cubes that would be invisible from the outside.
Explain why the outside view alone undercounts the volume.
activities.insight: Unseen interior and bottom-layer cubes are part of the volume; relying on visible faces undercounts the 3-D array.

checkQuestion: Show a box that is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm (or its net) and a pile of 1 cm³ blocks. Ask: 'How many 1 cm³ blocks are needed to fill this box completely — and how did you work it out?'
checkAnswer: 24 cubic centimetres. Each layer is a 4-by-3 array of 12 cubes and the box is 2 layers deep, so 12 × 2 = 24 (equivalently 4 × 3 × 2), counting the hidden lower layer as well as the top.
